families.prompt: A bag holds {r} {c1} and {b} {c2} {it}. You draw two without replacement. What is the chance both are {c1}? Give a fraction.

wrong.line: You used {r} out of {n} on both draws. Without replacement the second draw has one {c1} fewer and one item fewer.
You took one off the {c1} count but kept {n} on the bottom. The bag holds {n - 1} items for the second draw.

solution: The first is {c1} with chance $\tfrac{{{r}}}{{{n}}}$. One {c1} item has gone, so the second is {c1} with chance $\tfrac{{{r - 1}}}{{{n - 1}}}$.

families.prompt: A bag holds {r} {c1} and {b} {c2} {it}. You draw one, put it back, then draw again. What is the chance of {c1}, then {c2}? Give a fraction.

wrong.line: You took one off the bottom for the second draw. The item went back, so the bag holds {n} items both times.
You counted {c2} then {c1} as well. The question asks for {c1} first, then {c2}.

solution: The item goes back, so both draws use the same bag of {n}.

families.prompt: A bag holds {r} {c1} and {b} {c2} {it}. You draw three without replacement. What is the chance all three are {c1}? Give a fraction.

wrong.line: You used {r} out of {n} on every draw. Without replacement each draw has one {c1} fewer and one item fewer.
You took {c1} items off the top but kept {n} on the bottom. The bag shrinks by one each draw.

solution: Each draw has one {c1} fewer and one item fewer than the last.
